en: The Sūtra on the Birth of the Bodhicitta, in one fascicle, translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Jñānagupta of North India during the Great Sui Dynasty.
Thus have I heard: At one time, the Bhagavān was staying at Rājagṛha in the Kalandaka Bamboo Grove.

In the garden, he was accompanied by a great assembly of one hundred thousand bhikṣus, as well as an immeasurable, incalculable, and ineffable multitude of great bodhisattvas who had gathered from the ten directions.

At that time, in the great city of Rājagṛha, there was a brahmin of the Mahākāśyapa clan who, while asleep, dreamed that within Jambudvīpa there was a great lotus flower with a thousand petals. Its radiance illuminated the trichiliocosm, and it was composed of the most exquisite and supreme seven precious jewels.

Within the lotus, one sees a lunar disc; within that lunar disc, one further sees a man emitting great radiance that universally illumines all things. All sentient beings throughout these four continents who behold this light experience immense joy and boundless exultation, and all partake in happiness.
At that time, after the brahmin Kāśyapa had awakened from sleep, he recalled the events of his dream; his heart was filled with joy yet gave rise to doubt:
"What are the causes and conditions for this?
What exactly has occurred?"
"Previously, this unprecedented sign appeared, such as I have never heard before, just as I saw in my dream.
Having had this thought, he gave rise to a great joy such as he had never seen before, and further reflected thus:

"There is this śramaṇa Gautama; I have heard from others that he practiced austerities for six years, subdued the hosts of Māra, realized Great Bodhi, turned the wondrous Wheel of Dharma, and crushed all non-Buddhists. He is praised by all wise men, being intelligent, skillful, and knowledgeable regarding the characteristics of all phenomena."
"I should now go to that śramaṇa Gautama and inquire about the meaning of this dream.

Then, when the night had passed, the brahmin Kāśyapa departed from Rājagṛha for the Kalandaka Bamboo Grove; having arrived at the place where the Buddha was, he prostrated himself at the Buddha’s feet and withdrew to stand to one side.
Having stood to one side, he related to the Buddha exactly what he had seen in his dream.
When the brahmin had finished recounting the dream in detail, the World-Honored One then addressed the brahmin Kāśyapa, saying:
"O son of good family!
There are four kinds of auspicious dreams through which one attains the sublime Dharma. What are these four?
They are: dreaming of a lotus flower while asleep, or seeing a parasol, or seeing the lunar disc, or seeing the form of the Buddha.
Having seen this, one should rejoice, thinking: "I have encountered the supreme Dharma.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:
"If one sees a lotus flower in a dream, Or likewise sees a parasol in a dream;
Furthermore, if one sees the lunar disc within a dream, one shall obtain great benefit;
if one dreams of the Buddha’s form, his body adorned with all the perfect marks,
beings who see this should rejoice, for they should remember that he will surely become a Tamer of Men.
At that time, having heard these verses, the brahmin Kāśyapa again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
What constitutes this great benefit, such that all sentient beings might attain it and seek the path to bodhi?"
At that time, the Buddha said to the brahmin Kāśyapa:
"The great benefit is what is called omniscience; this is the benefit.
Then the brahmin Kāśyapa again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
Regarding what is called ‘the wisdom of all-knowledge,’ by what causes and conditions can it be attained?
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke in verse to the Brahmin Kāśyapa:
"I shall now proclaim a great benefit; O Brahmin, listen well.
If there is a beneficial union, one shall become a Honored One among bipeds.
Or one may become a Wheel-Turning King, sovereign over the four continents."
If sentient beings wish to become so, they must resolve upon bodhicitta.
If one wishes to become a Brahmā King, Attaining mastery over the multitudes,
Sentient beings who wish to do so Must resolve upon bodhicitta.
Whether in the desire realm or the form realm, in the formless realm or the higher realms,
sentient beings who wish to act [for their own benefit] must give rise to the bodhicitta.
If there are sentient beings who wish to become caravan leaders, [they too must do so].
To be a guide for the caravan leader, one must resolve to attain bodhicitta.
If there are sentient beings who wish to become a great light that destroys all darkness, they must resolve to attain bodhicitta.
If there are sentient beings who wish to extinguish all inversions,
as well as the three realms of existence and so forth, they must give rise to the bodhicitta.
If there are sentient beings who wish to extinguish all hindrances and obstructions, [they must give rise to the bodhicitta].
And for all unwholesome dharmas, one must resolve to attain bodhicitta.
If there are sentient beings who wish to extinguish ignorance and sever the net of craving and attachment,
they must resolve to attain bodhicitta.
If there are sentient beings who wish to extinguish existence and craving,
as well as defilement and its absence, they must give rise to the bodhicitta.
If there are sentient beings who wish to extinguish the pride of "I" and "mine," [they must give rise to the bodhicitta].
And regarding form, which gives rise to the conceit of "I," one must resolve to attain bodhicitta.
If there are sentient beings who wish to be free from arrogance,
as well as the conceits of health and life, they must resolve to attain bodhicitta.
If there are sentient beings who wish to extinguish the pride of old age and the pride of permanence regarding impermanence, they must give rise to the bodhicitta.
If there are sentient beings who wish to extinguish the pride of extensive learning, [they must give rise to the bodhicitta].
And regarding pride in one's observance of the precepts, one must resolve to attain bodhicitta.
If there are sentient beings who wish to extinguish pride in dwelling in the araṇya,
pride in begging for food, and all such prides, they must resolve to attain bodhicitta.
If there are sentient beings who wish to extinguish pride regarding their knowledge and pride regarding their fondness for rag-robes, they must give rise to the bodhicitta.
If there are sentient beings who wish to extinguish pride regarding their supernormal powers, [they must give rise to the bodhicitta].
Taking but a single meal constitutes purity; one must arouse the bodhicitta.
If there are sentient beings who wish to extinguish all pride and every pride regarding conditioned phenomena, they must arouse the bodhicitta.
If there are sentient beings who wish to make offerings to the Buddhas who have already entered parinirvāṇa,
they must first resolve their minds toward Bodhi.
If there are sentient beings who wish to make offerings to the Buddhas...
All Tathāgatas must first resolve upon the mind of enlightenment (bodhicitta).
If there are sentient beings who wish to turn the wheel of Dharma—
which none in the world can turn— they too must resolve upon the mind of enlightenment.
If there are sentient beings who wish to extinguish [defilements], they should indeed extinguish them;
they should contemplate what is to be contemplated and must resolve to generate the bodhicitta.
If there are sentient beings who wish to practice the brahma-faring, they should likewise do so.
At the beginning, middle, and end, one must resolve upon the bodhicitta.
If there are sentient beings who wish to gather all forms of diligence while wandering through the various realms of existence, they must resolve upon the bodhicitta.
If there are sentient beings who wish to speak of the suffering of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*),
and seeing that sentient beings undergo suffering, must give rise to the bodhicitta.
If there are sentient beings who [realize] that all phenomena are without self,
If one wishes to preach for the sake of sentient beings, one must generate the bodhicitta.
If there are sentient beings who wish to turn the wheel of Dharma and wish to touch supreme enlightenment, they must generate the bodhicitta.
If there are sentient beings who wish to proclaim the tranquil nirvāṇa and would attain supreme bodhi, they must first give rise to the bodhicitta.
Such merits as these can be obtained by those who resolve their minds upon awakening.
“O brahmin, having heard this, you should practice the path to bodhi.
At that time, having heard these verses, the brahmin Kāśyapa again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!”
"How much a mass of merit should one who has resolved upon bodhicitta gather?
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses to the Brahmin Kāśyapa:
"If all sentient beings in this buddha-field Were established in faith and maintained in ethical discipline..."
That most supreme mass of merit does not equal even a sixteenth part of the mind set on enlightenment.
Even if all sentient beings in this Buddha-field were made to abide in faith and practice the Dharma,
that most supreme mass of merit would still not equal even a sixteenth part of the mind set on enlightenment.
If one were to build monasteries throughout as many Buddha-fields as there are sands in the Ganges for the sake of seeking merit,
and further construct stupas as vast as Mount Sumeru, these would not equal even a sixteenth part of the mind set on the Way.
If there were Buddha-fields as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, and one were to bestow all manner of the seven treasures throughout them all—
the most supreme mass of merit resulting from such an act would not equal even a sixteenth part of the mind set on the Way.
As vast and high as Mount Cakravāḍa, One might build immeasurable stūpas for the Buddhas;
Yet beings who seek merit in such ways Do not equal even a sixteenth part of the mind set on the Way.
If all sentient beings were to carry, upon their heads or shoulders, for the duration of an entire kalpa,
a mass of supreme merit such as that, it would not equal even a sixteenth part of the mind set on the Way.
When such persons as these attain the supreme Dharma, and if they seek awakening to benefit sentient beings, those beings are the most excellent; they have no equal, let alone any superior.
Therefore, having heard these various dharmas, the wise person always gives rise to a mind that delights in the Dharma;
they shall obtain a boundless mass of great merit and swiftly realize the unsurpassed path.
At that time, the brahmin Kāśyapa again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
Is there any regression for one who has thus resolved their mind toward bodhicitta?”
At that time, the Buddha said to the brahmin Kāśyapa:
“One who thus gives rise to the bodhicitta shall never regress from liberation.”
However, in terms of their distinct natures, there are three kinds of bodhi.
What are these three? They are:
the bodhi of the śrāvaka, the bodhi of the pratyekabuddha, and the anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
“Great Brahmin! What is the awakening of the śrāvaka?

If a son or daughter of good family resolves upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, yet does not instruct others to resolve upon the bodhicitta, nor causes them to abide in it, nor explains such sūtras for them; nor personally upholds them, nor extensively explains their meaning to others; and even though they associate with such persons (*pudgala*), they do not serve or provide them with what is required.”

If there are those who come and those who do not come, one neither shows them respect nor gives rise to sympathetic joy toward them; by this cause and condition, the mind attains liberation—O Brahmin!
"This is what is called the enlightenment of a śrāvaka.
Furthermore, what is the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha?

If a son or daughter of good family generates the bodhicitta for themselves, yet does not teach others to generate the bodhicitta, does not cause others to abide in it, nor explains such sūtras for them; if they do not personally uphold [the teachings], nor extensively explain them to others, nor associate with such individuals (pudgala), nor serve and provide for their needs; [this is the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha]."

Whether there are those who come or those who do not come, one neither shows them respect nor rejoices in them; by means of these causes and conditions, one realizes pratyekabuddha-bodhi with the mind—therefore, it is called the path of the pratyekabuddha.
"Furthermore, what is this *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*?

If a son or daughter of good family personally resolves their mind toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, and likewise instructs others to resolve their minds toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, and having established them therein, further preaches such sūtras for others so that they may all receive, uphold, and draw near to such *pudgalas*, serving and making offerings to them; [this is *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*]."

Whether there are those who come or those who do not come, one should revere them all and give rise to sympathetic joy. Such liberation, which benefits oneself and others, is for the sake of the welfare of many, for the sake of the happiness of many, and out of compassion for the world to bring benefit and happiness to gods and humans alike; it is therefore called *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
For what reason is it called *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*?
Because there is nothing superior above it that can be sought, it is therefore called *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke in verse:
"Having personally resolved upon the Bodhi-mind, Yet not teaching others to receive and uphold it,
Because of the power of one’s own mind alone, One enters Parinirvāṇa later on."
Exerting oneself for one's own benefit, yet not teaching others to uphold [the Dharma], is therefore called a śramaṇa;
such a person is a disciple of the Buddha and a most excellent teacher.
Those who have resolved upon bodhicitta teach and transform others, giving rise to joy.
Therefore, having attained the Way by oneself, one understands the fruit and retribution thus.
Having achieved it for oneself but not for others, such a field of merit among all sages is named a Pratyekabuddha; O Brahmin, you should know this.
Having personally generated the bodhicitta, And further liberated many sentient beings,
Acting for the benefit of the world, He is thus named the Buddha, the Guide.
Having accomplished his own welfare, He further causes others to attain liberation.
"There is no distinction between this and that; therefore, it is called 'inconceivable.
At that time, the Brahmin Kāśyapa addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
“Is there a distinction between liberation and liberation?
The Buddha said, “Brāhmaṇa!”
There is no distinction between liberation and liberation;
there is no distinction between the path and the path;
yet there is a distinction between vehicles and vehicles.

For example, on a royal highway there may be those traveling in elephant carriages, those in horse carriages, and those in donkey carriages; they all travel along that road in succession and arrive together at the same city.
"Brahmin! What do you think?
Are there any distinctions among such vehicles as these?"
The brahmin said:
"Venerable World-Honored One!
Nevertheless, those various vehicles truly have distinctions."
The Buddha said, "So it is, so it is, brahmin!"

There are distinctions between the vehicle of the śrāvakas, the vehicle of the pratyekabuddhas, and the vehicle of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi; however, there is no distinction between the path and liberation.
"Brahmin! It is like the Ganges River, where three kinds of people go from this shore to the other shore.
As for the first person, he makes a raft out of grass and crosses by leaning upon it."
The second person crosses by means of a leather bag or a leather boat, leaning upon them;
the third person constructs a large ship and boards it to enter the river, carrying hundreds of thousands of people within that vessel.
The third person further commanded the eldest son to station himself and guard this boat, saying:
"For the sake of benefiting many people, you must ferry all sentient beings who come from this shore to the other shore."
“Brahmin! What do you think?
Is there any distinction regarding that ‘other shore’?”
The brahmin said,
“No, World-Honored One.”
The Buddha asked again:
"Brahmin, what do you think?"
"Is there a distinction between those vehicles?
The brahmin replied,
"The vehicles that are ridden indeed have distinctions."
The Buddha said: “So it is, so it is, brahmin!”
Nevertheless, Brahmin, there is indeed a distinction between the vehicle of the śrāvakas, the vehicle of the pratyekabuddhas, and the vehicle of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
Just as a first person, relying on a raft of grass, goes from this shore to the other shore alone and without a second— thus should one understand the enlightenment of the śrāvaka.
"O Brahmin, as for the second person, who relies upon a leather bag or a leather boat to cross from this shore to the other shore— pratyekabuddha-bodhi should be understood in this same way."
Just as a third person, having equipped a great ship together with a multitude of people, travels from this shore to the other shore, so too should the enlightenment of the Tathāgata be understood.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:
"The paths and liberations have none above them; Yet among all vehicles, there are distinctions.
The wise should thus make such comparisons, And take up the most excellent, the Supreme Vehicle."
"Such is the teaching on all phenomena; this is what the Perfectly Awakened One has declared.
Having discerned all phenomena, the Victor should train therein.
At that time, the brahmin Kāśyapa again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
How should a bodhisattva mahāsattva practice, and how should they establish mindfulness, in order to reach the Mahāyāna?
At that time, the Buddha addressed the brahmin Kāśyapa, speaking these words:
“Brahmin! Listen to this meaning:
if bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice according to their contemplation, they will reach the Mahāyāna.”
"Brahmin! If a son or daughter of good family personally resolves upon the mind of enlightenment and also teaches others to resolve upon the mind of enlightenment;
if they themselves delight in practice and exhort others to practice, establishing them therein, and further explain the meaning of such sūtras;..."
Regarding such individuals (pudgala), one should not come near them to attend to or serve them; rather, one should gather them through the four means of attraction (saṃgrahavastu).
What are these four?
"These are what are known as generosity, kind speech, beneficial action, and cooperation.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:
"Various kinds of great giving, All things that one possesses,"
In order to gather others into his fold, the fearless Bodhisattva manifests the path of guidance;
though sentient beings do not come to rely upon him,
he is able to repeatedly comfort them with words of sublime goodness.
For the sake of the peace and happiness of oneself and others,
may those beings who have been born in favorable realms always follow [the path] day and night.
May those sentient beings who lack faith be led to believe in the teachings, and may those who break the precepts be established in the discipline.
They cause the stingy to practice generosity, providing every skillful benefit.
They teach people to cultivate bodhi, remaining firm and ever-diligent.
Regarding matters of mutual benefit, the wise act according to these instructions.
One who possesses such wisdom is a guide for Bodhisattvas;
one who practices according to wisdom always delights in the Mahāyāna Dharma.
This courage is supreme; the wise should study it.
"Because of those supreme dharmas, the Most Victorious One has reached the further shore.
At that time, the brahmin Kāśyapa again addressed the Buddha in verse, saying:
"O Great Virtuous One, you have shown that practice; O Bodhisattvas, you are the true guides."
I shall study their conduct so as to attain the state of the Honored One among Two-Legged Beings.
For my sake, explain that conduct, as well as the basis for practicing such conduct;
may you, out of compassion, speak of this profound and vast awakening.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the brahmin Kāśyapa, saying:
"Excellent, brahmin!
Bodhisattvas have three kinds of practice."
What are the three?
They are the divine conduct, the brahminical conduct, and the noble conduct. O Brahmin!
Among these, what is called "divine conduct" (*devacāra*)?

If there are sons or daughters of good family who, with a compassionate physical action, a compassionate mental action, and a compassionate verbal action, pervade immeasurable worlds in the eastern direction until their compassionate conduct is fully established;

having performed this pervasion, they are further able to skillfully enter the south, west, north, the four intermediate directions, and the zenith and nadir, universally filling them all with compassionate physical, mental, and verbal actions—this is called divine conduct.
Among these, what is called the holy life (*brahmacarya*)?
It refers to the four immeasurables (*apramāṇa*). What are the four?
They are loving-kindness (*maitrī*), compassion (*karuṇā*), sympathetic joy (*muditā*), and equanimity (*upekṣā*); these are called the holy life.
"Brahmin! Among these, what is called 'noble practice'?
It refers to the three gates of liberation—what are the three?"
"Emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness—these are called the noble practices.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:
"The courageous one who practices with diligence, The guide of the Bodhisattvas,"
If one possesses the conduct of the devas, that person delights in bodhi.
The noble conduct and the Brahma-conduct—these are the practices taught by the Sages.
If there is one who practices them, that person attains the immovable.
At that time, the brahmin Kāśyapa again addressed the Buddha in verse, saying:
“I delight in the profound bodhi; now I ask the Great Guide:
how shall these beings in future ages accumulate all their various practices?”
For the sake of future sentient beings, I ask the World-Honored One regarding the Buddha’s bodhi; my mind is free from discrimination,
so that I may give rise to the aspiration for enlightenment in order to benefit all beings.
At that time, the World-Honored One again addressed the brahmin Kāśyapa in verse, saying:
"By preaching this sūtra, I cause [beings] to resolve upon great bodhi,
O brahmin!"
In the Buddha’s bodhi, there has never been any discrimination.
By preaching this sūtra, he causes [beings] to resolve upon great bodhi;
it can sever all doubts, responding in accordance with the questions of sentient beings.
By preaching this sūtra, may they be inspired toward great bodhicitta;
it can sever all doubts according to the inclinations of those sentient beings.
Those who hear this sutra will, in future ages, [attain...]
Able to practice great giving, they reach the other shore of dāna.
Those who are able to hear this sutra will, in future ages,
maintain the precepts without flaw and reach the other shore of śīla.
Those who hear this sutra will, in future ages,
practice patience for the sake of sentient beings and reach the further shore of patience.
Those who hear this sutra will, in future ages...
Exerting diligence for the sake of sentient beings, they reach the further shore of diligence.
Those who hear this sutra will, in future ages,
constantly enter various meditative concentrations and reach the further shore of dhyāna.
Those who hear this sutra, in future ages,
shall seek supreme wisdom for the sake of the multitude and reach the further shore of knowledge.
Having already made offerings and having compassion for sentient beings, they shall attain this.
Having heard this sutra, it shall reach their hands in future ages.
The bhikṣu dwelling in an araṇya who desires the Buddha’s bodhi—
those who hear this sutra shall be the very first to attain it in the future.
In the past, many hundreds of millions of Buddhas Already upheld this sutra for the benefit of all bodhisattvas, To inspire their resolve and aspiration.
If there be any brahmins Who desire and delight in the Buddha’s bodhi,
At that time, having attained faith, this sutra shall come into their hands.
I see those sentient beings and fully know all their deeds;
I also know their names, seeing them all without any hindrance.
"I could explain everything in full, yet I fear it would confuse those of the future;
apprehensive that they might give rise to various faults, I therefore speak but a small portion.
At that time, the brahmin Kāśyapa again addressed the Buddha in verse:
“Virtuous One, by this skillful upholding, may you give rise to a vast mind;
before long, I too shall become such a Great Being in this world.
As taught by the Guides of the past and the future,”
"To produce wholesome benefit for them, I abide in enlightenment.
At that time, the World-Honored One again replied to the brahmin in verse:
"For whom was it said that they abide in this wisdom?"
Having already known their mental dispositions, I shall now grant them this prediction:
those who have heard this sutra and stand before me now,
for them this sutra shall manifest in future lives.
If there are women who transcribe this sutra, this sutra shall remain in their hands, and they will be able to give rise to great bodhi.
As I have already said before: "The bhikṣu delights in the araṇya."
Having obtained this sutra in hand, it shall manifest before them in the future.
Upon hearing this sutra, the bhikṣu wept with sorrow, shedding tears like rain, and said:
"What karma did I perform in the past that I have now obtained such benefit in this life?"
Regarding such a sutra as this, I have never properly reflected upon it;
yet I have now received my prediction—by what karma was this fruit obtained?
In the past, when I was a brahmin, I lived in dependence upon a bhikṣu.
At that time, the bhikṣu was negligent as he recited this sūtra.
A brahmin heard him there; when it was time for his almsround, he went out weeping, making a vow in his heart at that moment.
I shall serve as a witness for the sūtras, their summarized meanings,
and their words, and I shall likewise provide protection.
By the fruit of those wholesome karmas, in the successive ages of the final dharma-ending period,
Having obtained this sūtra, they hold it in their hands.
At that time there was a bhikṣu, whose eyes were filled with tears of sorrowful weeping;
having then performed repentance, he later obtained this dharma of the sutra.
When former karma is exhausted, at that time signs appear;
within his sleep and dreams, he obtains this sūtra.
Regarding the various cycles of birth and death, which are deceptive and full of great terror—
This results from the power of Amitābha’s vows; such is the fruit thereof.
Monks who break the precepts are held in contempt by others;
with many such faults, they wander through great terrors.
"Thus, through having heard this sutra, one shall reach the end of these many evils and shall forever shine brightly thereafter.
At that time, the brahmin Kāśyapa again addressed the Buddha with these verses:
"This great sūtra causes one to resolve upon the Great Vehicle;
for my sake and for the sake of those in the future, please analyze and proclaim it extensively.
At that time, the World-Honored One again addressed the brahmin of the Kāśyapa clan in verse:
"All future sounds, even those I shall speak, these are the extensive scriptures; therefore you should know this.
When these great scriptures are spoken, they shall be known as the Āgamas."
This should be treated as a secret treasury, to be studied by the śrāvakas.
What is taught here, as well as that attained by others who have realized the Path—this is the mother of all sūtras; thus should the brahmin know it.
At that time, O bhikṣus!
There were the *Saṃyukta* and the *Dīrgha Āgama*, and also the one named the *Madhyama Āgama*;
at that time there was an *Āgama* complete in number, called the *Ekottara*.
Furthermore, he will preach miscellaneous sūtras, the three baskets as spoken by the śrāvakas,
and he shall also compose the Vinaya and the Abhidharma;
it is for these reasons that he shall be known as a bhikṣu among the three baskets.
Eighty-four thousand aggregates of Dharma have been taught by me;
all [teachings] emerge from this, and it is called the Supreme Sūtra.
Within it, the Śrāvakas are explained, as well as the Pratyekabuddhas.
The root of all wisdom, the inconceivable scripture;
whatever exists in the world, even that which has not yet appeared within the three realms—
the root of all merit arises from the generation of the bodhicitta.
The virtues of generosity and ethical discipline, The practices of patience and diligence,
And the supreme virtue of meditative concentration— These are well-expounded within this sutra;
As are the supreme virtues of wisdom, Liberation, patience, and tranquil extinction.
All these are manifested; they are well-expounded within this sutra.
Suffering, its origin, the path, and cessation are revealed herein.
All phenomena are the Buddha-dharma; this is what is taught in this sutra.
It speaks of all sufferings as impermanent, and also speaks of the dharma of non-self;
it speaks of the tranquility of nirvāṇa—this is found in this sūtra.
Herein, the śrāvakas are spoken of, along with the various causes and conditions upon which they rely.
This Mahāyāna sūtra encompasses all dharmas.
All dharmas are exceedingly vast, yet they reside within the bodhicitta;
this is the most supreme scripture, universally expounding the sūtras.
They see the Buddhas face to face, And hear them preaching the Dharma for their sake;
That they hear this at that very moment Is due to this sutra.
Among all sentient beings in the three realms, Few have heard this sutra.
"Having heard this, they give rise to love and joy, for the sake of seeking the Buddha Vehicle.
At that time, the brahmin Kāśyapa again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"How rare, World-Honored One!"

If sentient beings lack wisdom, and if they hear such unsurpassed and boundless [teachings]—even to the point that such beings will have no wisdom—and having heard such boundless and unsurpassed sūtras, they are unable to give rise to firm resolve and aspiration within this Dharma.
"Venerable World-Honored One!
By what causes and conditions does it come to pass that, although such a sublime Dharma exists, those sentient beings nevertheless let it go to waste?
At that time, the Buddha addressed that brahmin, saying:

"In this trichiliocosm, there are hundreds of koṭis—where 'koṭi' refers to ten million according to the Sui numbering system—of Māra palaces. Each of those Māras is surrounded by a retinue of Māra followers numbering in the koṭis. These Māras constantly apply skillful means, desiring to destroy this sutra; they create all manner of causes and conditions, and by virtue of those causes and conditions, they create various obstacles wherever this sutra may be."
Why is this? If all sentient beings within the trichiliocosm were to attain the fruit of arhatship,
yet there were some son or daughter of good family who, upon hearing this sūtra, were to resolve to attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
"Brāhmaṇa! For this reason, millions of Māras will diligently seek out expedient means wishing to destroy this sutra.
Why is that? Brāhmaṇa!"
This sūtra is the fundamental source of the seed-nature of all dharmas; for this reason, millions of māras diligently seek out expedient means, desiring to extinguish this scripture.
At that time, the Buddha told the brahmin:
"There is now a sūtra called 'The Assembly for Destroying Māra.
If you receive, uphold, read, and recite it, you will immediately be able to destroy that assembly of the Māra-devas."
"Brāhmaṇa! Just as when the orb of the sun appears, it is able to extinguish all gloom and darkness; even so, Brāhmaṇa!"
When the *Sūtra on Shattering the Assembly of Māras* was being preached, all the māras vanished and did not appear.
O Brāhmaṇa! What is called the *Sūtra on Shattering the Assembly of Māras*?
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke this dhāraṇī, saying:

“Tad te | Anumodana | Bodhisamādāpana | Vuta | Yuvuta | Tatravuta | Nikhaṃgamaka | Parapa | Tarapa | Dhu | Dhuraga-makamana | Virima | Masuma | Hrivagama | Vidarama | Darukuma | Aramiramira | Ikakhara-nayū | ‘Brahman!’”
This dhāraṇī is that which the Buddhas,
the World-Honored Ones, of the past, future, and present have all together proclaimed in this Sūtra on the Assembly for Destroying the Multitudes of Māras. O Brāhmaṇa!

When this Sūtra for Shattering the Assembly of Māras was being preached, all the palaces of Māra shook, trembled, quaked, swayed, and swelled; all the Māras each fell headlong from their respective seats, unable to speak.

Why is this so? Because they constantly acted to the detriment of many people and constantly caused suffering to many, depriving them of their welfare; for these reasons, they now experience such terrifying retribution.

Because the Buddha, the World-Honored One, constantly bestows happiness upon all sentient beings—even through loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity—he causes those Māras and their like to give rise to terror.

"O Brahmin! If there should be anyone capable of turning this *sūtra* on the arousal of the bodhicitta, no obstacles shall exist for that person—whether from devas, nāgas, yakṣas, humans or non-humans, Māras, sons of Māra, or the retinues of Māra; nor from water, fire, swords, or staves; nor from evil-doers, or various predatory beasts; nor from physical afflictions or mental sufferings. It is impossible that such things should befall them."

Why is this? Because those sons and daughters of good family constantly perform deeds for the benefit and peace of many people; because they constantly act out of compassion for many people; and because they provide protection for all devas and humans—it should be understood that this is due to the power of the practice of loving-kindness of those sons and daughters of good family.
"O Brahmin!

Because those sons and daughters of good family do not engage in misconduct of body, do not engage in misconduct of speech, and do not engage in misconduct of mind, those various painful matters do not afflict their bodies, nor do they afflict their minds."
"O Brahmin! By means of these causes and conditions, one is able to extinguish all suffering.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to reiterate this meaning, spoke in verse:
“The Māra exerts himself against this sutra, desiring to destroy it; therefore,
the Tamer now speaks this scripture to cause the Māra to become utterly bewildered,
so that he gathers his hosts and sits trembling.”
Gazing at one another, they cannot speak; this is the retribution for their evil deeds.
Because they terrified sentient beings and constantly harbored a mind intent on doing harm, they have fallen into perversion; therefore, they receive this manifest retribution.
When one is united with compassion, speaks with a joyful mind,
and teaches the Dharma with equanimity, all malicious intentions are utterly dispersed.
One subdues all the Māras and scatters their demonic hosts.
The yakṣas and various spirits will naturally all fall away.
His power and staff cannot harm him; water and fire cannot sweep him away or burn him.
Even spoken curses and poisons are unable to cause him injury.
Neither bodily affliction nor mental distress shall ever befall them;
they shall always abide in the vows they have undertaken, with body and speech remaining thus.
They shall block all evil paths and remain far removed from every hardship.
All Māras are utterly subdued for the sake of preaching this sutra.
Regarding the skillful wisdom of all dharmas, if one wishes to cross to the other shore, one must hear this scripture;
having heard it, one is then able to practice it.
"If one can study this sutra, the fearless bodhisattvas will attain the supreme awakening of bodhi; this is the phrase that leads toward bodhi.

When the Buddha spoke this sutra, the brahmin Kāśyapa and the entire great assembly—including gandharvas, devas, asuras, and others—having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
